note: Paul's most sustained argument, indexed in two sections: the gospel of righteousness by faith (1-8) and Israel, the life of the community, and the greetings (9-16). The Scriptural Appendix cites 1:20 for C24 and 11:33-34 for the Discipline of Unknowing.
coverage_note: Left unindexed by design: 9:22-23 ('vessels of wrath made for destruction') and 11:7-10 (hardening, with the quotation from Psalm 69) are indexed only through the entries that frame them; the index anchors what these passages say about mercy and the limits of human reply, and does not adjudicate the doctrine of election. 1:24-27 is part of the 1:18-32 argument and is not given its own entry. 14:24-26 (the doxology in WEB numbering), 16:21-24 (closing greetings) and 16:25-27 (blank in the WEB) are not indexed separately.

entries.pericope: That I with you may be encouraged in you, each of us by the other's faith
entries.connection: The apostle writing to a church he has never visited says he wants to give them something, and corrects himself at once: 'that is, that I with you may be encouraged in you, each of us by the other's faith, both yours and mine.' Encouragement as mutual rather than handed down. C13's shared life, offered on equal terms.

entries.pericope: Knowing God, they didn't glorify him as God, neither gave thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix cites 1:20 for the claim that 'the evidence has been on public display throughout': 'the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made.' C24's landscape as testimony. The failure that follows is traced in sequence, and its first step is ingratitude: 'knowing God, they didn't glorify him as God, neither gave thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.' C07's darkened lens produced by the condition of the heart, and C21's anatomy of a descent in which each stage — 'God gave them up,' three times — is the consequence of the last. The list of vices that closes the chapter is part of the argument the index anchors, not a separate set of tags.

entries.pericope: In that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things
entries.connection: Having described the failures of others, Paul turns on the reader who has been nodding along: 'Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things.' Self-Accusation's discipline of sequence — one's own portion first — applied to the very act of judging. C03's beam and speck. 'Or do you despise the riches of his goodness… not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?' And the standard is C04's: 'it isn't the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers,' with a conscience 'accusing or else excusing' them.

entries.pericope: You therefore who teach another, don't you teach yourself?… whose praise is not from men, but from God
entries.connection: The one who knows the law and teaches it is asked the audit's question about consistency, five times: 'You therefore who teach another, don't you teach yourself? You who preach that a man shouldn't steal, do you steal?…' The Moral Audit's fifth area — where private conduct differs from public — pressed on the teacher specifically. And the outward sign read inwardly: 'circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God' — C06's reading, and the hidden praise C23 waits for.

entries.pericope: There is no one righteous; no, not one… The way of peace, they haven't known
entries.connection: A chain of psalm verses describing the human condition by its speech and its feet: 'Their throat is an open tomb… whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood… The way of peace, they haven't known.' 'That every mouth may be closed.' C04's audit applied to everyone at once, and C21's root found in every heart rather than in a few.

entries.pericope: All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace… Where then is the boasting? It is excluded
entries.connection: 'For there is no distinction, for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace.' C19's door, with every distinction removed at the threshold. And the consequence for the person who walks through it: 'Where then is the boasting? It is excluded.' C22's humility as the natural posture of the forgiven.

entries.pericope: Who in hope believed against hope… he didn't consider his own body, already having been worn out
entries.connection: Abraham 'believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness' — before the sign, before the law, before the son. 'Who in hope believed against hope… Without being weakened in faith, he didn't consider his own body, already having been worn out… Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn't waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith.' C19's righteousness received as gift, and C25's long wait sustained not by evidence but by a promise.

entries.pericope: Suffering works perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope… while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us
entries.connection: A staircase like 2 Peter's, but built out of trouble: 'we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering works perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope.' Each stage produces the next and none can be skipped, which is the Discipline of Gradualism's claim. Then the ground of the whole curriculum's ethic of enemy-love, stated as what God is like: 'God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies, we were reconciled.' C03 grounds Non-Retaliation 'not in effectiveness but in what God is like,' and this is what God is like.

entries.pericope: Where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly
entries.connection: Adam and Christ set side by side: one trespass, one act of righteousness; death reigning through one, life through the other. 'The law came in besides, that the trespass might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly.' C19's door, wider than any failure that might be brought to it.

entries.pericope: Don't let sin reign in your mortal body… present yourselves to God, as alive from the dead
entries.connection: 'Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be!' Baptism as death and burial, and the new life as a walk: 'that… we also might walk in newness of life.' C26's change of nature, and its daily form, C20's: 'Therefore don't let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Neither present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness.' What is not handed over at the gate does not rule.

entries.pericope: To whom you present yourselves as servants to obedience, his servants you are… What fruit then did you have at that time?
entries.connection: 'Don't you know that to whom you present yourselves as servants to obedience, his servants you are whom you obey?' C21's diagnostic maxim — what you obey is what masters you, whatever you call it — and the backward look that tests it: 'What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.' Fruit as the measure, C11's image, set against 'your fruit of sanctification.' 'The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life.'

entries.pericope: So that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter
entries.connection: The analogy of a widow freed from the law of her husband: the believer has died to the law 'that we might bring forth fruit to God… so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.' C06's movement from the letter's surface to the spirit beneath it.

entries.pericope: For I don't practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do… What a wretched man I am!
entries.connection: The most searching account of moral failure from the inside in all of scripture. It begins with a single commandment — 'You shall not covet' — and traces how desire used the command against itself: 'sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting.' Then the divided self: 'For I don't practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do… For the good which I desire, I don't do; but the evil which I don't desire, that I practice… What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?' Interior Diagnosis follows a failure back through its phases to the place it entered; this is that tracing done honestly, ending not in a technique but in a cry and a thanksgiving. C21's anatomy and C26's divided heart, which C26 promises will be made whole.

entries.pericope: There is therefore now no condemnation… you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!
entries.connection: The answer to the cry of 7:24: 'There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.' C19's door at its widest. The life that follows is an indwelling — 'if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you… If Christ is in you' — which is C11's, and its mark is a cry of belonging rather than fear: 'you didn't receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!' 'The mind of the Spirit is life and peace.'

entries.pericope: For we don't know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can't be uttered
entries.connection: The whole creation 'groans and travails in pain together until now,' and 'we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting.' Groaning as the honest sound of a world not yet healed — C19's hope held inside it: 'hope that is seen is not hope… we wait for it with patience.' And then the deepest admission in the letter: 'we don't know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can't be uttered.' The Discipline of Unknowing reaches even into prayer, and Sacred Lament is carried on our behalf when we cannot form it ourselves (both at medium; the passage describes rather than commands). C09's secret place, where even the words are given.

entries.pericope: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?
entries.connection: 'If God is for us, who can be against us?… Who is he who condemns?… Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?' Every threat named and none sufficient: 'neither death, nor life… nor things present, nor things to come… nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God.' C19's security, and C22's quiet soul grounded in something no circumstance reaches.

entries.pericope: I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers' sake
entries.connection: Paul begins the hardest section of the letter under oath — 'I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me' — and what he swears to is grief: 'great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.' Grief for the people who, at the time of writing, were the ones opposing him from city to city. 'I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers' sake.' Shedding Harshness asks who stands outside the circle of concern; Paul's circle includes the people who drove him out, and he would trade his own place to bring them in. Tagged at medium: he exemplifies the widened circle rather than teaching it. C03's love for the one who sets himself against you, and C27's boundless reach.

entries.pericope: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy… O man, who are you to reply against God?
entries.connection: The argument from election: Isaac and not Ishmael, Jacob before either twin had 'done anything good or bad.' 'So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.' The index anchors two things here and no more. First, that mercy is not earned by the runner — C19's door. Second, the posture Paul demands of the objector: 'But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, "Why did you make me like this?"' The Discipline of Unknowing at its least comfortable — the passage closes the question rather than answering it, and the practice is to let it stay closed. The index does not adjudicate the doctrine of election or the 'vessels of wrath' (9:22); see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge… seeking to establish their own righteousness
entries.connection: 'I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn't subject themselves to the righteousness of God.' Zeal as the counterfeit of the thing it is zealous for: those who 'didn't follow after righteousness' attained it, and those who pursued it 'as it were by works' stumbled. C19's door refused because the one standing at it insists on building his own. And C06's distinction between the earnest surface and the seeing eye — sincerity is not sight.

entries.pericope: The word is near you, in your mouth, and in your heart… How will they hear without a preacher?
entries.connection: 'Don't say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?"… The word is near you, in your mouth, and in your heart.' C19's door is not up a mountain or down a pit; it is at the level of the mouth. 'For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him.' Then the chain of dependence that makes the door reachable: call, believe, hear, preach, be sent. 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace.' C16's service as carriage — someone has to walk the message to the door. And God's patience in the closing line: 'All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.'

entries.pericope: I am left alone… I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal
entries.connection: Elijah's complaint — 'I am left alone, and they seek my life' — and God's answer: 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Seven thousand the prophet had never heard of, whose faithfulness was invisible even to the most faithful man in Israel. C23's hidden life in its plainest form: unrecorded, unnoticed, counted. And a correction to the prophet's sense of isolation, which C13 would recognise — the remnant is larger than the one who feels alone in it can see. The quotation at 11:9-10 belongs to the argument about hardening and is not indexed separately.

entries.pericope: Don't boast over the branches… it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you. Don't be conceited, but fear
entries.connection: The olive tree: natural branches broken off, a wild shoot grafted in 'contrary to nature.' Paul turns at once on the grafted branch before it can congratulate itself: 'don't boast over the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you… Don't be conceited, but fear.' C11's vine image from the other side — the branch does not hold up the tree — and C22's humility as the only safe posture for anyone who has been given what they did not grow. 'See then the goodness and severity of God… if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off.'

entries.pericope: So that you won't be wise in your own conceits… For God has shut up all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all
entries.connection: The mystery is disclosed for a stated purpose — 'so that you won't be wise in your own conceits' — and its shape is mercy passed from hand to hand: 'as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience, even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy.' Then the sentence the whole argument has been building toward: 'For God has shut up all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all.' C19's door, held open by the same failure in everyone. 'The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.'

entries.pericope: Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix cites 11:33-34 because the most rigorous argument in the New Testament ends 'in wonder rather than mastery, anchoring The Discipline of Unknowing.' Three chapters of argument about election and mercy, and the arguer stops: 'Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?' The practice modelled by the one person best placed to claim he had mastered the subject. C24's wonder, and C22's rest in not needing to.

entries.pericope: Present your bodies a living sacrifice… be transformed by the renewing of your mind
entries.connection: 'Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.' The ethic that follows is grounded in mercy received — 'therefore… by the mercies of God' — not in obligation. Then the change from the inside: 'Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.' C26's transformation of nature, and C07's cleansing of the lens: a renewed mind is what makes the good visible enough to test.

entries.pericope: Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably… he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness
entries.connection: 'I say… to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.' C22's sober self-estimate — not low, but accurate. One body, many members, differing gifts, and each gift with its manner: 'he who gives, let him do it with liberality; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.' C13's shared life and C16's service, each member doing its own part and not another's.

entries.pericope: Let love be without hypocrisy… in honor preferring one another… contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality
entries.connection: 'Let love be without hypocrisy' — C12's proof, love that can be checked against conduct. A run of short commands describing a community's ordinary week: 'In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate one to another; in honor preferring one another; not lagging in diligence… rejoicing in hope; enduring in troubles; continuing steadfastly in prayer; contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality.' Habitual Almsgiving is the regular sharing of resources directed toward actual need; 'contributing to the needs' prescribes it as a standing habit (medium — one clause in a list). 'In honor preferring one another' is the principle beneath Deferential Seating but does not prescribe the practice itself, so PR25 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Bless those who persecute you… Repay no one evil for evil… Don't seek revenge… If your enemy is hungry, feed him… overcome evil with good
entries.connection: The fullest apostolic statement of the Sermon's ethic. 'Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don't curse.' 'Repay no one evil for evil.' 'Don't seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God's wrath. For it is written, "Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord"' — Deuteronomy 32:35, which the Deuteronomy entry anchors, here turned into the ground of the believer's restraint. 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him… Don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.' Non-Retaliation in its two halves: the refusal and the positive act. Shedding Harshness in the blessing of the persecutor. And the Architecture of Peace exactly as A1 defines it — act toward repair even if the other person does not: 'If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.' The limit is honest; the responsibility is one's own half. 'Weep with those who weep' sits in the middle, C27's wide heart, and the C03 chapter is where all of this lives.

entries.pericope: Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities… Give therefore to everyone what you owe
entries.connection: 'Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities… for conscience' sake. For this reason you also pay taxes… Give therefore to everyone what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due; customs to whom customs; respect to whom respect; honor to whom honor.' The Citizen-Stranger's first half — 'obey the laws gladly' — written to believers in the capital of the empire that would kill the writer. Indexed with the guard the practice itself carries: 'let your ultimate loyalty rest above any human decree.' The passage describes authority as 'a servant of God to you for good'; it does not address an authority that commands evil, and Acts 5:29 ('We must obey God rather than men') stands beside it in the index. The entry anchors the ordinary posture, not a doctrine of unlimited obedience.

entries.pericope: Owe no one anything, except to love one another… Love doesn't harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law
entries.connection: 'Owe no one anything, except to love one another' — the one debt that is never paid off. The commandments 'are all summed up in this saying, namely, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." Love doesn't harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.' C03's blueprint, with the law read as love's specification rather than its rival, and C29's whole heart, in which the commands are no longer external.

entries.pericope: The night is far gone, and the day is near… make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts
entries.connection: 'It is already time for you to awaken out of sleep… The night is far gone, and the day is near. Let's therefore throw off the works of darkness, and let's put on the armor of light.' Then the gatekeeper's instruction: 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.' Watchfulness holds that destructive thoughts do their damage 'during the hospitality, not the arrival' — making no provision is refusing to set the table. C20's watchman, and the list of 'strife and jealousy' beside 'drunkenness' as works done in the dark.

entries.pericope: Who are you who judge another's servant?… each one of us will give account of himself to God
entries.connection: A real dispute — food and holy days — and Paul refuses to settle it by declaring a winner. 'Don't let him who eats despise him who doesn't eat. Don't let him who doesn't eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him. Who are you who judge another's servant? To his own lord he stands or falls.' Both errors named: contempt from the strong, judgment from the scrupulous. And the sentence that turns every accuser back on himself: 'So then each one of us will give account of himself to God.' Self-Accusation's discipline of sequence — attend to your own account — set as the answer to disagreement within the church (medium). C15's peace and C03's refusal to judge, with C04's mirror pointed where it belongs.

entries.pericope: That no man put a stumbling block in his brother's way… let us follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up
entries.connection: 'Let's not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother's way.' Paul concedes the strong are right on the merits — 'nothing is unclean of itself' — and then makes being right beside the point: 'Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don't destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.' The Architecture of Peace changes the objective from 'how do I prevail' to 'what would repair look like': 'let us follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up.' Liberty limited by love, voluntarily. The Sacrifice of Routine runs the other direction (one's discipline yielding to a guest's ease) and is not tagged; neither is Covering Weakness, which concerns public embarrassment over a mistake. The doxology the WEB prints as 14:24-26 is not indexed separately.

entries.pericope: We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. For even Christ didn't please himself
entries.connection: 'Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up. For even Christ didn't please himself.' C16's logic of service — the stronger party carries the load — grounded in Christ's own example. 'Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you.' C14's household and C15's peace, ending in a prayer that the divided community might 'with one accord… with one mouth glorify the God and Father.'

entries.pericope: I will not dare to speak of any things except those which Christ worked through me… that I might not build on another's foundation
entries.connection: Paul's account of his own work is careful about credit in both directions. Of the Romans: 'I myself am also persuaded about you… that you yourselves are full of goodness… able also to admonish others.' Of himself: 'I will not dare to speak of any things except those which Christ worked through me.' And his ambition, stated as a rule against taking credit for another's labour: 'making it my aim to preach the Good News, not where Christ was already named, that I might not build on another's foundation.' C22's honest estimate of one's own part, and C16's service that does not compete.

entries.pericope: A certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem… they owe it to them also to serve them in fleshly things
entries.connection: The letter's travel plans pause for a collection. 'It has been the good pleasure of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem.' An organised, deliberate sharing of resources across a great distance, directed at actual need — Habitual Almsgiving at the scale of churches — and Paul delays his own mission to deliver it in person. The reason given is a debt of gratitude: 'if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in fleshly things.' Then a request that the Romans 'strive together with me in your prayers' — he asks for help openly.

entries.pericope: Greet Mary, who labored much for us… Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored much in the Lord
entries.connection: Twenty-six names, most mentioned nowhere else in scripture, each with a word about what they did: Phoebe, 'a helper of many, and of my own self'; Prisca and Aquila, 'who for my life, laid down their own necks'; Mary, 'who labored much for us'; Tryphaena and Tryphosa, 'who labor in the Lord'; Rufus's mother, 'and mine.' Households, fellow prisoners, women and men named as co-workers. The church as C13 actually describes it — ordinary people faithful in ordinary places — and C23's hidden labour, preserved here only because someone thought to say thank you by name. The specific praise resembles Verbal Almsgiving, but A1 aims that practice at the discouraged and isolated, and nothing here says these people were; PR21 is not tagged. The closing greetings (16:21-24, including Tertius the scribe and Gaius the host) belong to the same picture and are not indexed separately.

entries.pericope: By their smooth and flattering speech, they deceive the hearts of the innocent… wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil
entries.connection: 'Look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling… For those who are such don't serve our Lord, Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by their smooth and flattering speech, they deceive the hearts of the innocent.' C08's test of the teacher by whom he serves, with smooth speech as the warning sign rather than the credential. And the posture asked of the church: 'I desire to have you wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil' — C20's gate kept by knowing the good well rather than studying the evil.
